en_lines.text: Chapter four: the contraction principle, the engine of this part.

To solve cosine of x equals x, just iterate: start anywhere, apply the cosine, and apply it again. On the graph, bounce between the curve and the diagonal: the path spirals in on the crossing. Why it works: on this interval the cosine's slope is at most sine of one, about 0.84, so each application shrinks distances by that factor. The errors shrink geometrically, and the theorem we're about to prove even predicts a bound for them in advance, the last column. The solution is 0.7390851332, the only one there is.

The theorem, Rudin 9.23: on a complete metric space, a map that shrinks every distance by a factor c less than one has exactly one fixed point. Start anywhere and iterate. Each step is at most c times the one before, so the n-th step is at most c to the n times the first. Adding up the steps between the n-th point and any later one gives a geometric series: every later point lies in a disc of radius c to the n over one minus c times the first step. The discs shrink to nothing, so the sequence is Cauchy. The space is complete, so the points converge, and because the map is continuous, the limit is fixed. And two fixed points would have to be closer to each other than they are, so there's only one.

Completeness can't be dropped. The map x over two plus one over x sends rationals to rationals, and on the interval from one to two it shrinks distances by at least half. Iterate from one: three halves, seventeen twelfths, five hundred seventy-seven over four hundred eight. The iterates form a Cauchy sequence, but the point they close in on is the square root of two, the hole in the rationals from Part 1. Among the rationals, there is no fixed point at all.

And Newton's method from the opening is a contraction too. Its step is the map g of x equals x minus f over f prime, and at a simple root its derivative is zero. For the square root of two, g is flat where it crosses the diagonal, so near the root it shrinks distances by a factor as small as we like. That's why Newton's method is so fast: each step contracts harder than the one before, the error squares, and the number of correct digits doubles.

zh_lines.text: 第四章：压缩映射原理，这一部分的引擎。
要解cos x等于x，只要迭代：从任意一点出发，取余弦，再取一次余弦。在图上，就是在曲线和对角线之间来回弹：路径螺旋着收向交点。为什么行得通：在这个区间上，余弦的斜率至多是sin 1，大约0.84，所以每作用一次，距离都至多变为原来的0.84倍。误差按几何级数缩小，而我们马上要证明的定理，甚至能事先给出误差的上界，就是最后一列。解是0.7390851332，而且只有这一个。

定理，鲁丁9.23：在完备度量空间上，如果一个映射把每段距离都至多缩小为原来的c倍，其中c小于1，那么它恰好有一个不动点。从任意一点出发迭代。每一步至多是前一步的c倍，所以第n步至多是第一步的c的n次方倍。把第n个点与之后任意一个点之间的各步加起来，得到一个几何级数：之后的每个点都落在一个圆盘里，半径是c的n次方除以（1减c），再乘以第一步。这些圆盘缩得什么都不剩，所以这个序列是柯西序列。空间是完备的，所以这些点收敛；又因为映射是连续的，极限就是不动点。而如果有两个不动点，它们之间的距离就得比它们之间的距离还小，所以只有一个。
完备性不能去掉。映射“二分之x加x分之1”把有理数送到有理数，而且在1到2的区间上，它把距离至少缩小一半。从1开始迭代：二分之三，十二分之十七，四百零八分之五百七十七。这些迭代值构成一个柯西序列，可它们逼近的那个点是根号2，也就是第1部分里有理数中的那个洞。在有理数里，根本没有不动点。
开场里的牛顿法也是一个压缩映射。它的一步就是映射g(x)等于x减去f除以f的导数，而在单根处，这个映射的导数是0。对根号2来说，g在穿过对角线的地方是平的，所以在根附近，它缩小距离的比例要多小有多小。这就是牛顿法这么快的原因：每一步都比前一步压缩得更狠，误差被平方，正确的位数翻一番。

cases.title: Part 13 · Router load collapse
cases.text: We built one: Part ten's character model, with its hidden layer split into 8 experts and 2 used for each character. Train it, and watch how the characters are shared out. Left alone, the router plays favourites: the busiest expert ends up with 3.3 times its fair share, while others starve. It's a rich-get-richer loop: a favoured expert gets more practice, gets better, and gets chosen even more. Starved experts are wasted parameters.
cases.summary: Moved vo.wait_until('a') after the 2,000-step router load replay so the heatmap fills in while the narrator says 'train it', eliminating an 8.6 s sparse stretch.

cases.title: Part 10 · Maximal update (μP)
cases.text: Greg Yang asked how to scale a network so that every layer keeps learning features, at any width. His answer, the maximal update parametrization, mu-P, rescales the initialization and learning rate of each layer by the width. In plain terms: as the network widens, shrink each layer's starting weights and step size, so that every layer keeps changing by about the same amount. Sweep the learning rate at three widths, the usual way. At our small sizes, the best rate barely moves. Now in mu-P. What shows here is what mu-P is for: its widest model is the best of all, 2.56 bits against 2.66 the usual way, because every layer keeps learning. At large scale the usual way's best rate does drift, and mu-P holds it still: Yang and colleagues tuned a forty-million-parameter model and copied its settings to a GPT-3 of six point seven billion, which beat the original.
cases.summary: Faded in the μP scaling card on the first word of the paragraph instead of waiting for <bookmark mark='m'/>, removing 14.8 s of bare-header dead air.

cases.title: Part 10 · Grokking Fourier modes
cases.text: What is the rule it found? Look at the vectors it learned for the numbers. Most of their weight sits on 9 frequencies out of 48: waves around the clock. A frequency places the 97 numbers evenly around a circle, in order: at frequency one, going round once; at frequency five, going round five times. Seen along their main directions, the numbers lie on circles; here they are forming during training, and the circles appear just as the test accuracy climbs. The network turns each number into an angle, and adds numbers by adding angles, as a clock does. Neel Nanda and colleagues worked this out in 2023, one of the first complete explanations of what a trained network computes. Part twenty takes that idea to real models.

cases.title: Part 20 · Chain-of-thought faithfulness
cases.text: This matters for part seventeen's reasoning models. Their chains of thought look like a window into their thinking. But are they? One test: slip a hint into the question, and see if the model uses it, then check whether its chain of thought admits it. Most of the time, it doesn't: a quarter of the time for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, under two fifths for DeepSeek-R1. The written chain is not always the real computation. That's why reading the inside directly, with the tools of this part, matters.
